```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

This guide shows how to check whether variables share a long-run
relationship in panel data, with the tests of Westerlund (2007) and the
function `pcoint_westerlund()`. It assumes that you know what a regression
and a p-value are, and nothing more. Technical words are explained when
they first appear, and again in the glossary at the end.

```{r setup}
library(panelcointr)
```

## 1. The question

Many economic series grow over time: income, prices, health spending. Two
growing series will look related even when they have nothing to do with
each other, so a regression on their levels can be badly misleading. Here
are two series of pure noise that never influence each other:

```{r spurious}
set.seed(1)
a <- cumsum(rnorm(100))   # a "random walk": each value is the last one plus noise
b <- cumsum(rnorm(100))   # another one, unrelated to a
coef(summary(lm(a ~ b)))
```

The t-value of `b` is far from zero, yet `b` has no effect on `a`. This is a
**spurious regression** (Granger and Newbold 1974). It happens because each
series wanders off without a fixed level to come back to. Such a series is
called **non-stationary**, or is said to have a **unit root**. A shock to it
never fades away: it shifts the series for good.

Some wandering series really are linked, though: they wander *together*.
Picture a person walking a dog on a long leash (Murray 1994). Each of them
wanders around, but the leash stops them from drifting far apart. Series
like these are **cointegrated**: each one wanders, but the gap between them
(the leash) stays within bounds. When they drift apart, something pulls them
back towards each other. That pull is called **error correction**.

The Westerlund tests ask one question: **is there error correction?** If
there is, the variables are cointegrated.

* The **null hypothesis** (what the test assumes until the data say
  otherwise) is *no cointegration*: no leash.
* A **small p-value** (below 0.05, say) is evidence *for* cointegration.

Why use a **panel**, that is, many units (countries, regions, firms) observed
over time? With a single country you often have 30 to 50 yearly
observations, which is too few to tell a leash from no leash. Pooling the
information of many countries makes the test much more reliable.

## 2. The data

The package includes the data of the paper's example: per-capita health care
expenditure and GDP, in logs, for 20 OECD countries from 1970 to 2001. The
question is whether health spending and income move together in the long
run.

```{r data}
head(hce)
```

The data are in **long format**: one row per country and year. `ctr`
identifies the country (1 to 20; the source does not name them) and `year`
counts the years (1 is 1970, 32 is 2001). These two columns are the **panel
index**. `loghex` and `loggdp` are the logs of health spending and GDP.

It always helps to look at the data first. Each line is one country:

```{r plot-data, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5}
years <- 1969 + sort(unique(hce$year))
hex <- matrix(hce$loghex, nrow = length(years))   # one column per country
gdp <- matrix(hce$loggdp, nrow = length(years))
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
matplot(years, hex, type = "l", lty = 1, col = "grey40",
        xlab = "Year", ylab = "log", main = "Health spending per capita")
matplot(years, gdp, type = "l", lty = 1, col = "grey40",
        xlab = "Year", ylab = "log", main = "GDP per capita")
par(op)
```

Both series climb steadily in every country: they have upward **trends**.
Keep this in mind for the `deterministic` setting below.

## 3. Running the test

```{r first}
fit <- pcoint_westerlund(loghex ~ loggdp, data = hce, index = c("ctr", "year"),
                         deterministic = "trend", lags = c(1, 3), leads = c(0, 3))
```

What each argument means:

* `loghex ~ loggdp` has the form `y ~ x`. The test asks whether `y` (here
  health spending) corrects towards its long-run relationship with `x`, so
  put on the left the variable you expect to adjust. You can use several
  explanatory variables, as in `y ~ x1 + x2` (up to six for the standard
  p-values).
* `data` and `index`: the data frame and the names of its unit and time
  columns.
* `deterministic`: what the long-run relationship contains besides the
  variables. `"constant"` (the default) allows a different average level for
  each country; `"trend"` adds a straight-line trend for each country. Both
  of our series trend upwards, so we use `"trend"`. `"none"` is rarely
  appropriate.
* `lags = c(1, 3)`: the number of past changes of the variables in each
  country's equation, which capture short-run movements. A range such as
  `c(1, 3)` lets each country pick its own number between 1 and 3 with an
  **information criterion** (AIC by default), a rule that balances fit
  against complexity. `lags` has no default, because results can depend on
  it: choose a sensible range and check that your conclusion does not hinge
  on it.
* `leads = c(0, 3)`: the number of future changes of `x` in the equation.
  Leads protect the test when `x` itself reacts to `y` (here, if health
  spending also affected GDP). The default, 0, includes none.

## 4. Reading the output

```{r print}
fit
```

Line by line:

* **H0: no cointegration** reminds you of the null hypothesis.
* **20 units, 1 regressor ...** describes what was used: 20 countries, one
  explanatory variable, 32 years, and a constant and trend.
* **Lags** and **Leads**: each country chose between 1 and 3 lags, and on
  average it chose about 2. The same goes for the leads.
* **Bartlett bandwidth** is a technical setting used inside two of the
  statistics. The default is fine.
* **The table** has four statistics, which answer slightly different
  questions:
  * `Gt` and `Ga`, the **group-mean** statistics, test each country
    separately and then average the results. Rejecting means that *at
    least some* countries error-correct.
  * `Pt` and `Pa`, the **panel** statistics, pool all countries and assume
    they adjust at the same speed. Rejecting means that the panel *as a
    whole* error-corrects.
  * `Value` is the raw statistic. `Z-value` puts it on a common scale (a
    standard normal distribution); the more negative it is, the stronger
    the evidence of cointegration. `P-value` is the probability of getting
    a Z-value at least this negative if there were no cointegration.

All four p-values are below 0.05, which seems to say that health spending
and income are cointegrated. **But these p-values rest on an assumption
that is doubtful here**, as the next section explains.

## 5. A crucial check: countries are not independent

The p-values above assume that what happens in one country is unrelated to
what happens in the others. With OECD countries this is hard to believe:
oil shocks, recessions and new medical technologies hit many countries at
the same time. Units that move together like this show **cross-section
dependence**, and it can make the standard p-values much too small.

The remedy is the **bootstrap**. The function builds many artificial data
sets in which, by construction, there is no cointegration, but in which the
countries still move together as they do in the real data (it reshuffles
whole years, so that all countries share the same draw). It computes the
statistics on each artificial data set and then asks how often they are as
negative as the real ones. That share is the **robust p-value**.

`bootstrap = 499` asks for 499 artificial data sets. Because the bootstrap
is random, call `set.seed()` first, so that you get the same numbers every
time you run the code:

```{r boot}
set.seed(2007)
fit_boot <- pcoint_westerlund(loghex ~ loggdp, data = hce, index = c("ctr", "year"),
                              deterministic = "trend", lags = c(1, 3), leads = c(0, 3),
                              bootstrap = 499)
fit_boot
```

The new column, `Robust P`, tells a different story: the robust p-values
range from `r min(fit_boot$statistics$p_boot)` to
`r max(fit_boot$statistics$p_boot)`, and none is below 0.05. Once we allow
the countries to move together, **the evidence of cointegration is weak**.
With only 32 years and countries hit by the same shocks, the data cannot
tell clearly whether there is a leash.

**Which p-values should you report?** Whenever your units can be hit by
common shocks (nearly always with countries, regions, or firms in the same
market), use the robust ones. The standard p-values are fine only when the
units are plausibly independent. For final results, use more replications,
such as `bootstrap = 999`; the computation is fast.

`plot()` shows the bootstrap distribution of each statistic as a histogram.
The solid line is the real statistic and the dashed line the 5% critical
value: the real statistic must fall to the left of the dashed line to reject
at the 5% level. Here all four lie to the right of their dashed lines:

```{r plot-boot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
plot(fit_boot)
```

## 6. Looking inside the results

`summary()` adds more detail:

```{r summary}
s <- summary(fit_boot)
s
```

* **Bootstrap critical values**: thresholds for each statistic. A statistic
  below its 5% critical value rejects the null at the 5% level.
* **Selected lags and leads**: how many countries chose each number.
* **Mean-group error-correction model**: averages of the countries' own
  estimates. They describe the relationship *if* the variables are
  cointegrated, so after the bootstrap results above, read them with care.
  * *Long run*: the `loggdp` estimate,
    `r round(s$mean_group$long_run["loggdp", "estimate"], 2)`, says that a
    1% higher GDP goes with about
    `r round(s$mean_group$long_run["loggdp", "estimate"], 2)`% higher health
    spending in the long run, on average across countries.
  * *Short run*: `ec`, `r round(s$mean_group$short_run["ec", "estimate"], 2)`,
    is the average **speed of adjustment**: each year, about
    `r round(-100 * s$mean_group$short_run["ec", "estimate"])`% of any gap
    between health spending and its long-run level is closed. A value near
    0 would mean no error correction.
* **Units**: one row per country. `alpha` is that country's speed of
  adjustment and `t_alpha` its t-ratio (more negative means stronger evidence
  of error correction in that country). `lags` and `leads` are the orders it
  chose.

The pieces of the result are ordinary R objects that you can use in your
own tables and plots:

```{r pieces}
fit_boot$statistics
head(fit_boot$units)
```

## 7. Practical checklist

* **Data.** Long format, one row per unit and period. The time variable
  must step by one within each unit. Missing values at the start or end of a
  unit are dropped; gaps in the middle are an error. Units may cover
  different periods.
* **Before testing.** The variables should be non-stationary: cointegration
  is only about series that wander. Panel unit root tests, such as
  `plm::purtest()`, can check this.
* **`deterministic`.** Use `"trend"` if the series trend, `"constant"`
  otherwise.
* **`lags` and `leads`.** Give ranges and let each unit choose. Check that
  the conclusion survives a different range.
* **Cross-section dependence.** Use `bootstrap` and report the robust
  p-values, with `set.seed()` for reproducibility.
* **Group-mean vs panel statistics.** If `Gt` and `Ga` reject but `Pt` and
  `Pa` do not, only some units may error-correct. If the panel statistics
  reject but the group-mean ones do not, the evidence comes from pooling.
* **Short panels.** With few time periods (here 32), conclusions are
  fragile. Say so when you report them.

If your units share strong common shocks or have sudden breaks (a reform, a
crisis), the companion guide to `pcoint_banerjee()`,
`vignette("banerjee", package = "panelcointr")`, covers a test that models
both explicitly.

## 8. Going further (optional)

### The model behind the test

For each unit $i$ the test estimates an **error-correction model**:

$$
\Delta y_{it} = \delta_i' d_t + \alpha_i y_{i,t-1} + \lambda_i' x_{i,t-1}
  + \sum_{j=1}^{p_i} \alpha_{ij} \Delta y_{i,t-j}
  + \sum_{j=-q_i}^{p_i} \gamma_{ij}' \Delta x_{i,t-j} + e_{it}.
$$

$\Delta$ means "change from the previous period" and $d_t$ holds the
constant and trend. The key coefficient is $\alpha_i$, the speed of
adjustment. If $\alpha_i < 0$, then whenever $y$ is above its long-run level
it tends to fall back: that is error correction. The null hypothesis is
$\alpha_i = 0$ for every unit. `Gt` and `Ga` average the unit-level t-ratios
and (suitably scaled) estimates of $\alpha_i$; `Pt` and `Pa` estimate one
common $\alpha$ from all units together. The lags ($p_i$) and leads ($q_i$) are the short-run terms set by
`lags` and `leads`.

### Matching Stata's xtwest

The Stata command `xtwest` (Persyn and Westerlund 2008) departs from the
paper in a few details, for example in how it chooses the lags. By default
`pcoint_westerlund()` follows the paper; `compat = "xtwest"` reproduces
`xtwest`, and `compat = "xtwest_westerlund"` its `westerlund` option. With
the three calls published by Persyn and Westerlund (2008), the results match
their output:

```{r xtwest}
runs <- list(
  list(lags = 1, leads = 1, lrwindow = 3, compat = "xtwest"),
  list(lags = c(1, 2), leads = c(0, 1), lrwindow = 2, compat = "xtwest"),
  list(lags = c(1, 3), leads = c(0, 3), lrwindow = 3, compat = "xtwest_westerlund")
)
published <- rbind(c(-2.681, -10.927, -12.035, -10.524),
                   c(-2.736, -11.254, -12.859, -11.773),
                   c(-4.082, -27.702, -12.969, -22.470))
ours <- t(sapply(runs, function(a) {
  r <- do.call(pcoint_westerlund,
               c(list(loghex ~ loggdp, data = hce, index = c("ctr", "year"),
                      deterministic = "trend"), a))
  r$statistics$value
}))
colnames(published) <- colnames(ours) <- c("Gt", "Ga", "Pt", "Pa")
knitr::kable(cbind(run = 1:3, round(ours, 3)), caption = "panelcointr")
knitr::kable(cbind(run = 1:3, published), caption = "Published xtwest output")
```

The only difference is the last digit of `Ga` in the second call: the value
is -11.2535, which `xtwest` prints as -11.254 because Stata stores its
intermediate results in single precision. `?westerlund_control` lists every
difference between the paper and `xtwest`, and lets you switch each one
separately.

## Glossary

* **Bootstrap**: a way to get p-values by simulating many artificial data
  sets that resemble the real one but satisfy the null hypothesis.
* **Cointegration**: two or more non-stationary series that move together
  in the long run, so that the gap between them stays within bounds.
* **Cross-section dependence**: units that move together because they are
  hit by the same shocks.
* **Error correction**: the tendency of a variable to move back towards its
  long-run relationship with others after a deviation.
* **Information criterion (AIC, BIC)**: a score that rewards fit and
  penalises extra terms, used to pick the number of lags.
* **Lags and leads**: past and future values of a variable's changes.
* **Long format**: one row per unit and period, with the unit and time in
  their own columns.
* **Non-stationary (unit root)**: a series that wanders without returning to
  a fixed level or trend; shocks to it are permanent.
* **Null hypothesis**: the statement a test assumes until the data provide
  enough evidence against it. Here: no cointegration.
* **Panel data**: the same units (countries, firms) observed over several
  periods.
* **P-value**: the probability of a result at least as extreme as the one
  observed if the null hypothesis were true. Small values are evidence
  against the null.
* **Spurious regression**: a regression that finds a "significant" link
  between unrelated non-stationary series.

## References

Granger, C. W. J. and Newbold, P. (1974). Spurious regressions in
econometrics. *Journal of Econometrics* 2(2), 111-120.

Murray, M. P. (1994). A drunk and her dog: an illustration of cointegration
and error correction. *The American Statistician* 48(1), 37-39.

Persyn, D. and Westerlund, J. (2008). Error-correction-based cointegration
tests for panel data. *Stata Journal* 8(2), 232-241.

Westerlund, J. (2007). Testing for error correction in panel data.
*Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics* 69(6), 709-748.
